name: How Medicine Learned to Heal
description: From skull drilling and bloodletting to vaccines, antibiotics and gene editing: the long road by which doctors learned what works and what harms.

checkpoints.name: Healers and guesses
checkpoints.note: For thousands of years healers drilled skulls, bled patients and used herbs, from Chinese needles to Andean bark. Some methods worked and many harmed, and nobody knew what caused disease until the microscope era.

checkpoints.name: Germs, needles and sleep
checkpoints.note: Jenner showed that cowpox prevents smallpox, anaesthesia let surgeons work slowly, and Pasteur and others proved that germs cause disease. X-rays and aspirin arrived at the end of the century.

checkpoints.name: The wonder drugs
checkpoints.note: Insulin and penicillin turned deadly illnesses into treatable ones, and machines such as the iron lung and the kidney dialyser kept patients alive. Some fashionable treatments, such as lobotomy, later proved tragic mistakes.

checkpoints.name: Machines, transplants and the pill
checkpoints.note: Polio vaccines emptied the wards, pacemakers and transplants repaired hearts, scanners looked inside the body, and the pill and IVF changed family life. The thalidomide disaster led to tougher drug testing.

checkpoints.name: Reading and editing life
checkpoints.note: Medicine turned to genes and information. Gene editing with CRISPR promised cures for inherited disease, and mRNA vaccines were designed and approved within a year to fight a new virus in 2020.
